pairs.original_question: What happens to an ETF's assets if its sponsor goes bankrupt?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, for an ordinary US '40 Act ETF whose fund and adviser/sponsor are separate entities, does sponsor insolvency itself give the sponsor's creditors the portfolio or wipe out the shares? Distinguish asset separation from a guaranteed outcome in every insolvency.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: The portfolio belongs to the fund, separately from its adviser; adviser creditors do not acquire a claim on that portfolio just because the adviser fails. Sponsor failure therefore does not by itself wipe out ETF shares. [ICI presentation to the Federal Reserve, “Protecting Fund Assets — Custody”](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/rr-commpublic/ici_meeting_20110104.pdf#page=1).

**Confidence: high** for asset separation; **medium** for the resulting insolvency conclusion, which is an inference for an ordinary separate fund/adviser structure. This is not a guarantee against investment losses or a conclusion about every insolvency case. Do not extend it to an ETN, which is issuer debt. A successor adviser, merger or liquidation is case-specific, not established by this source.

citations.section: Question-led candidates (2026-11-05) — QL-01, Research draft; source links embedded in key points

pairs.original_question: Does an investor lose the investment when an ETF closes?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, what normally happens to a US '40 Act ETF investor's holding when the ETF liquidates? Distinguish receiving remaining proceeds from losing the whole investment, and address amount, timing and taxable-account consequences without assuming a fund-specific timetable.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: Closure normally means selling the assets and paying the remaining proceeds proportionately to shareholders. It does not automatically mean losing the whole investment; the amount and payment date can differ from the last NAV or exchange price. An investor can normally sell before trading ends. [SEC fund-liquidation bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-96).

In one filed 2026 liquidation, shareholders receive NAV after charges, taxes, expenses and liabilities, with possible final income/gain distributions; taxable holders can realize a gain or loss. [One + One ETF liquidation supplement, March 13, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1884021/000121390026027879/ea0281711-02_497.htm). General tax principle: liquidation distributions recover basis, with excess taxable as capital gain; a loss may await the final distribution. [IRS Publication 550, “Liquidating Distributions”](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550).
**Confidence: high.** The filing is an example, not a universal liquidation timetable or allocation of closing costs.

pairs.original_question: How can an investor assess whether a small or new ETF is likely to close?
pairs.sharpened_question: For a small, newly launched US '40 Act ETF over its next year, what sponsor-economics and seed-capital indicators would you assess for closure risk? Explain indicators rather than predict a guaranteed closure or survival probability.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: Fixed operating costs mean a small fund can lose money at any reasonable fee; small and young funds are exposed to closure risk.
The sponsor bears break-even risk through the entity paying costs. Assess its willingness and ability to support losses, rather than treating size alone as a guaranteed closure prediction.

Market-maker seed is temporary inventory that can be redeemed; investor seed is more lasting, but subsidized seed investors can leave. A series-trust board can replace the adviser or liquidate the fund.

pairs.original_question: How is an ETF expense ratio collected from investors?
key_points: Operating expenses come out of fund assets and reduce returns; they are indirect investor costs rather than a separate investor bill. The prospectus fee table states the annual expense ratio. [SEC fees bulletin](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins/updated).

For ETFs, the costs accrue through daily deductions reflected in NAV. The annual rate is not a charge taken in full each day. [ICI, ETF expenses and fees, 2025, section V](https://www.ici.org/files/2025/per31-07.pdf).
**Confidence: high.** Daily accrual and the service provider's actual payment date are different things; the latter follows the contract.

pairs.original_question: Why can an ETF be more tax efficient than a mutual fund holding the same stocks?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, why can an in-kind US equity ETF taxed as an IRS RIC distribute fewer capital gains than a standalone cash-dealing mutual fund holding the same stocks, for a US taxable investor? State the limits of the tax benefit.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: An in-kind redemption transfers appreciated securities instead of selling them for cash; IRC 852(b)(6) provides fund-level nonrecognition on a qualifying shareholder-demanded redemption.
Low-basis lots can leave the portfolio, reducing embedded gains and subsequent distributions. Mutual fund cash redemptions more often require portfolio sales.
This is not an ETF-only legal exemption, a guarantee of no distributions, or exemption of the investor from tax on selling shares. In-kind benefits depend on deliverable assets and the transaction.

pairs.original_question: Can a mutual fund benefit from the tax efficiency of its ETF share class?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, for a US IRS RIC already permitted to operate ETF and mutual fund classes sharing one portfolio, can ETF-class in-kind redemptions benefit mutual fund class shareholders? Explain the mechanism and limits, without assuming every fund has share-class relief.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: ETF and mutual fund classes own the same portfolio. Removing appreciated, low-basis securities through ETF in-kind redemptions can reduce gains distributed to either class.
This removes embedded gains, without stepping up the basis of securities left behind. Cash sales can still generate gains; mutual fund cash flows can impose gains and costs on ETF holders.
The potential shared benefit is not guaranteed and depends on strategy and practical in-kind capacity. The fund-level rule does not exempt investor or AP gains.

pairs.original_question: Is an ETF's exchange trading volume enough to judge its liquidity?
pairs.sharpened_question: For a US ETF, is historical exchange share volume alone enough to assess liquidity for a new order? Explain the creation/redemption mechanism and which additional observable liquidity indicators to examine; do not promise execution capacity.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: Exchange volume measures trading in existing shares. APs can create additional shares or redeem them against a basket, so historic share volume alone does not measure the capacity to meet a new order. [ICI ETF basics, creation/redemption and arbitrage](https://www.ici.org/faqs/faqs_etfs).

Proposed assessment: examine quoted spreads and depth, underlying-market liquidity and AP/market-maker activity as well as share volume. Underlying liquidity affects spreads; IDC suggests monitoring spreads, volume and intermediary activity. [IDC oversight paper, ETF design and trading](https://www.idc.org/idc/issues/types/etf/publications/ci.idc_12_etfs).
**Confidence: high** for the mechanism; **medium** for this practical assessment, a synthesis rather than a guaranteed execution-capacity measure.

pairs.original_question: What keeps an ETF's market price close to its underlying asset value?
key_points: APs exchange baskets for ETF shares in creations, and return ETF shares for baskets in redemptions.
When market price deviates from NAV, profitable creation/redemption arbitrage pulls price back toward portfolio value; APs often act for market makers.
This is an economic mechanism, not a guaranteed equality of price and NAV.

pairs.original_question: How do creations and redemptions change the number of ETF shares outstanding?
key_points: Creation issues new ETF shares to the AP in exchange for a basket, increasing shares outstanding.
Redemption returns shares to the fund and destroys them, reducing shares outstanding.
Secondary-market trades transfer existing shares between investors and do not themselves change shares outstanding.

pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: In ordinary US ETF dealing, APs transact directly with the fund in creation units; retail investors trade existing shares through brokers on exchanges.
An ordinary retail sale is a secondary-market transaction, not a direct redemption with the fund. The prompt excludes reorganization, merger, conversion and liquidation exceptions.

pairs.original_question: Who can be an authorized participant, and what agreement is needed?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, for a US Rule 6c-11 ETF, what clearing/settlement eligibility and written agreement does an AP need? Distinguish the rule's permitted counterparties from the parties in the bank's reviewed US agreement forms.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: Rule 6c-11 permits an AP agreement with the ETF itself or one of its service providers.
In the reviewed US forms, the distributor and AP are main counterparties; the transfer agent countersigns, and the trust is a third-party beneficiary, sometimes signing for specified provisions.
The reviewed forms require NSCC netting membership for the clearing process and/or DTC participation outside it. Eligibility is not synonymous with being a market maker.

pairs.original_question: Are APs paid by the ETF sponsor, and must they keep creating and redeeming?
key_points: AP status does not require ongoing creations or redemptions, and the ETF/sponsor does not pay the AP for that role. Dealer APs earn through dealing; agency APs can charge clients for processing creations/redemptions. [IDC 2025 primer, p. 4](https://www.idc.org/system/files/2025-09/25-idc-etf-primer.pdf#page=5).

**Confidence: high.** This does not describe a separate market-maker quoting contract. See the fee-conflict proposal below: the fund's transaction fee is a cost charged to the AP, not AP compensation.

pairs.original_question: Why might a creation or redemption use cash instead of securities?
pairs.sharpened_question: For a US ETF whose strategy uses futures or OTC derivatives, why might creations or redemptions require cash rather than delivery of those positions? Contrast this with deliverable securities; do not assume every derivative is treated identically.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: In-kind delivery requires assets that can actually be transferred. The note identifies stocks, bonds and more recently options as deliverable examples.
The note identifies futures and OTC derivatives as outside custom in-kind transfers; a fund built on them has to transact for cash.
Cash dealing means the fund must trade rather than simply transfer securities, limiting the practical in-kind tax benefit. Do not generalize to all derivatives or all bonds.

pairs.original_question: Where can an investor obtain an ETF's daily basket or portfolio composition file?

pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: The fund website's daily portfolio download is the public starting point, but holdings are not necessarily the creation/redemption basket. Rule 6c-11 requires public holdings disclosure, not publication of every transaction basket. [Rule 6c-11(c)(1)–(3)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/270.6c-11).

NSCC distributes the PCF through its participant workflow. key_points: APs create and redeem with the fund in the primary market; market makers quote bids and offers and provide secondary-market liquidity.
Market makers manage inventory by creating/redeeming through APs. One firm can perform both roles, but the roles are distinct.
An LMM is designated for a particular ETF with quoting commitments; do not assume all market makers are APs.

pairs.sharpened_question: For a new US sponsor planning one ordinary ETF, with limited fixed-cost budget and no existing trust, board or servicing infrastructure, how should it compare a series-trust platform with building its own trust? Include the control trade-off and avoid assuming one answer suits every sponsor.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: A third-party series trust supplies an existing board, officers and service providers, spreading fixed governance and servicing costs across funds.
The sponsor gives up control of those parties; the board can replace the adviser or liquidate the fund. The sponsor can be adviser, sub-adviser or contractual partner.

For the stated small sponsor seeking one launch without governance infrastructure, a platform is a plausible fit; retain the control-versus-fixed-cost trade-off rather than declaring a universal winner.

pairs.original_question: How much does it cost to launch and operate an ETF?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, for one ordinary US equity ETF on a third-party platform under a unitary fee, budgeted in USD, which one-time and recurring cost categories and payer allocations should the sponsor establish? Distinguish seed assets from expenditure and explain break-even at a positive retained margin; do not invent a current vendor quote or universal dollar range.
pairs.change_note: Material narrowing: replaces unsupported current launch-price request with budgeting categories, payer allocation and break-even model. No defensible current all-in USD range in draft; reviewer/Rafa must accept this revised task.
key_points: Separate initial seed assets from money spent launching and running the business. The Act's ordinary initial public-offering condition is $100,000 of net worth, subject to its alternative provisions; that is not a quoted launch bill or a commercial break-even asset level. [Investment Company Act §14(a)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/80a-14).

Cost allocation is contractual: in Lazard's filed response, the manager bears the new ETF's organization costs without recoupment, and pays trustees directly under its unitary fee. [Lazard SEC correspondence, comments 11–12, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2051630/000093041325001085/filename1.htm).

**Draft decision aid (analytical, not a sourced market quote):** budget one-time legal/filing/setup work plus recurring servicing, listing, index and sales costs, then identify who pays each. Sponsor break-even assets ≈ annual fixed costs ÷ (retained fee rate minus variable cost rate), only when that margin is positive. **Confidence: high** for the cited legal/contract facts; **medium** for the simplified model. **Unverified:** a representative current dollar price or all-in launch/annual-cost range; do not promote the older interview's price as a market standard.

pairs.original_question: How long does an ETF launch take?
pairs.sharpened_question: As of 2026-11-06, for a new ordinary ETF series added to an existing US trust by a Rule 485(a) post-effective amendment, with no separate exemptive relief needed, what filing-effectiveness period normally applies, and why is it not an end-to-end launch guarantee? Distinguish initial registration of a new trust.
pairs.change_note: Material narrowing: replaces generic launch duration with the documented new-series filing clock and its limits. No universal commercial timeline supported; reviewer/Rafa must accept this revised task.
key_points: Adding a series by post-effective amendment normally has a 75-day automatic-effectiveness period; other material amendments normally use 60 days. The rule allows designated later dates and SEC acceleration. These are filing clocks, not promised end-to-end launch times. [Rule 485(a)(1)–(3)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/230.485).

A filed example elects the 75-day route and states that shares cannot be sold before effectiveness. [Simplify registration amendment, January 30, 2024, cover](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1810747/000182912624000561/simplifyetf_485apos.htm).

**Confidence: high.** Preparatory work, exchange readiness and any separate relief add their own time; **unverified:** a universal commercial launch estimate. Do not present 75 days as a guaranteed launch deadline or as the rule for a new trust's initial registration.

pairs.original_question: What should a board investigate when an ETF persistently trades at a premium or discount?

Check contemporaneous valuation/market hours, peers, underlying trading frictions and AP/market-maker participation; propose inquiry and corrective options rather than a single presumed cause or mandatory numerical trigger.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: Request causes and corrective options for persistent deviations; review spreads against peers and AP/market-maker participation. These are IDC's suggested inquiries. [IDC oversight paper, “Trading of ETF Shares”](https://www.idc.org/idc/issues/types/etf/publications/ci.idc_12_etfs).

**Proposed diagnosis (medium; synthesis):** test stale NAV inputs/market-hour differences, underlying trading costs and impediments to creation/redemption before assuming an arbitrage failure. **Confidence: high** for suggested monitoring; **medium** for the diagnostic sequence. The 2% website trigger (QL-25) is not a safe-harbor tolerance or a general board-meeting trigger.

pairs.original_question: What risks does an ETF's securities-lending program create, and how can they be reduced?
pairs.sharpened_question: For ETF securities lending, distinguish borrower/default, collateral-shortfall and cash-reinvestment risks and controls. Separate the bank's US iShares example from UCITS recall/collateral rules; do not promise collateral eliminates losses.
pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: US ('40 Act), iShares example: borrower failure can delay recovery or leave collateral short of replacement cost; investing cash collateral can itself lose money. Collateral is maintained at least equal to the current market value of securities lent; these controls do not remove loss risk. [iShares SAI, “Securities Lending,” pp. 16–17 of PDF](https://www.ishares.com/us/literature/sai/sai-ishares-us-etf-10-31.pdf#page=17).

UCITS: maintain the ability to recall loans; collateral needs daily valuation, liquidity, credit quality, diversification and appropriate haircuts. Noncash collateral cannot be reinvested; cash reinvestment is restricted and must be diversified. [ESMA guidelines, paragraphs 30 and 43–47](https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/library/2015/11/esma-2014-0011-01-00_en_0.pdf).
**Confidence: high.** US example terms are not UCITS rules; collateral-reinvestment loss is distinct from borrower default.

pairs.change_note: Scope and grading task made explicit; see sharpened wording.
key_points: Disclose the transparency policy and where portfolio/iNAV information is available in the prospectus, KID/KIID and marketing. [2026 regulations, Reg. 88(3)–(4)](https://www.centralbank.ie/docs/default-source/regulation/industry-market-sectors/funds/ucits/s-i-316-of-2026---central-bank-%28supervision-and-enforcement%29-act-2013-%28section-48%281%29%29-%28undertakings-for-collective-investment-in-transferable-securities%29-regul.pdf#page=64).

CBI permits daily holdings on a nondiscriminatory basis, or periodic holdings with daily arbitrage information available nondiscriminatorily to APs/market makers, prospectus disclosure of that information, procedures for impaired arbitrage and investor information requests, and public quarter-end holdings within 30 business days.
